pedagogy.summary: Children move from comparing mass to QUANTIFYING it: expressing mass as a number of units — first non-standard (this book balances 5 cubes), then standard (grams, kilograms) — and reading a simple dial/scale. The balance gives equivalence (the object balances N identical units); reading a graduated scale means valuing the intervals, not counting marks.
bestPractices: Use a balance to find how many IDENTICAL units balance the object (equivalence), recording as number + unit ('5 cubes', '200 g')
Insist units are identical — mixing cube sizes breaks the count (the unit-size principle: a larger unit gives a smaller count)
When reading a dial/scale, first work out what one interval is worth, then count intervals (spaces) to the pointer, not the marks
Estimate first, then check by measuring
Keep it practical; wait for the balance beam to settle before reading
keyRepresentations: Balance with identical unit-weights on one pan
commonMisconceptions: Uses non-identical units yet counts 'more units = heavier' (unit-size ignorance)
Reads a scale by counting marks rather than valuing intervals; misreads a pointer between graduations
Thinks the count itself is the mass regardless of which unit was used
Reads before the balance settles / uses a mix of unit sizes

learn.summary: Children move from comparing mass to quantifying it: expressing mass as a number of units — first non-standard (this book balances 5 cubes), then standard (grams, kilograms) — and reading a simple dial or scale. A balance shows equivalence (the object balances N identical units); reading a graduated scale means valuing the intervals, not counting marks. The key insight is that a larger unit gives a smaller count for the same object.

activities.title: Balance it with identical units
feedback: If a count is reported while the beam is still moving, prompt: wait for the beam to settle, then read. If it settles tipped to one side, it is not balanced, so add or remove a cube; if no whole number of cubes levels it exactly, record 'about' or 'between' two counts.
If cubes of mixed sizes were used, point out that the count only means something when every unit is identical; redo with one size.
If the estimate was far off, that is fine — the point is to compare your estimate with the measured count and notice the gap.
activities.rationale: Equivalence via balancing is a concrete route into quantifying mass and underpins later standard-unit work. Recording as number-plus-unit anchors the idea that the unit matters.
sourceClaims: NCETM mastery tasks assess mass via balance equivalence ('this box weighs 10 kg, how much does each tin weigh?') and via reading dial/kitchen scales to compare masses ('what is the mass of two red bags? which is heavier, red or green? explain'); the Year 1 Big Idea introduces equivalence ('how many cubes are equivalent to the mass of the teddy?').
learnerActions: Place a book (or other object) on one pan of a balance.

Add identical unit-weights (e.g. interlocking cubes) one at a time to the other pan until the beam levels, or is as near level as you can get; if one more cube tips it the other way, the object is between two counts.

Wait for the beam to settle before reading, then count the cubes and record the result as a number with its unit, e.g. '8 cubes', or 'about 8 cubes' / 'between 8 and 9 cubes' if it never quite levels.
Before you start adding cubes, check every cube is the same size; set aside any odd-sized ones.
Before adding any cubes, estimate how many you expect; after measuring, compare your estimate with the measured count.
activities.intendedInsight: Mass can be quantified as a number of identical units that balance the object; the record is a number plus a unit, not just a number.

activities.title: Same book, different unit size
feedback: If the child says the smaller big-cube count means the book is now lighter or has changed, show one big cube balancing several small cubes, so one big = many small; then the smaller count for the same book makes sense.
If the child claims 15 small cubes is heavier than 10 big cubes just because 15 > 10, compare the actual units directly on the balance: you cannot compare counts made with different-sized units.
Correct reasoning to reinforce: 'bigger cubes are heavier, so fewer of them balance the same book'.
activities.rationale: Directly targets unit-size ignorance by letting the child watch the count drop for an unchanged object. The inverse relationship between unit size and count is a core measurement idea, and discrete counting can otherwise convince children that unit size is irrelevant.
sourceClaims: The larger the unit, the fewer units in a given measurement (inverse relationship between unit size and count); counting discrete items can wrongly convince children that unit size doesn't matter, when in measurement it is critical.
learnerActions: Measure the SAME book again, this time using larger unit-weights.
Count how many large units balance the book and compare with the earlier count of small units.
Say aloud why the number is different even though the book has not changed.
Discuss: can both counts be right at the same time — for example '5 big cubes' and '12 small cubes' for the same book? Explain how.
Place one large unit on one pan and add small units on the other until it balances, or is as close as possible — count about how many small units equal one large unit.
Answer: if you used really tiny units instead, would the number be bigger or smaller? Why?
activities.intendedInsight: A larger unit means fewer units are needed to balance the same object; the count changes because the unit changed, not because the mass changed. Conversely, smaller units give a larger count.

activities.title: Read the dial by valuing the intervals
feedback: If the child counts the lines/marks to get the number, show that the value lives in the spaces between marks: count intervals, not lines.
If the child is stuck when the pointer is between marks, read to the nearest graduation and name the interval value first.
Prompt to check: how did you decide one interval is worth 100 g? Look at the labelled numbers on the scale.
activities.rationale: Scale-reading errors from counting marks instead of valuing intervals are structurally the same slip as misreading a ruler; establishing interval value first prevents it.
sourceClaims: NCETM mastery tasks assess mass via balance equivalence ('this box weighs 10 kg, how much does each tin weigh?') and via reading dial/kitchen scales to compare masses ('what is the mass of two red bags? which is heavier, red or green? explain'); the Year 1 Big Idea introduces equivalence ('how many cubes are equivalent to the mass of the teddy?').
learnerActions: Look at a dial or kitchen scale marked at regular intervals (e.g. a mark every 100 g).
First work out what ONE interval is worth, e.g. the gap between two marks is 100 g.
Count the intervals (the spaces) from zero up to the pointer, not the marks, to find the mass — e.g. three intervals of 100 g means 300 g.
Read to the nearest graduation when the pointer falls between two marks.
Explain how you knew each mark meant 100 g and not 1 g.
activities.intendedInsight: A graduated scale is read like a number line: establish the value of one interval, then count intervals to the pointer — this is the same skill as reading a ruler.

activities.title: Compare and order masses from readings
feedback: If the child tries to compare counts taken with different-sized units, remind them comparisons only work when the units match.
If ordering is reversed, line up the recorded numbers and check which is larger, then match the symbol.
Encourage a spoken reason for each comparison, not just the symbol.
activities.rationale: Comparing and ordering with >, <, = is an explicit curriculum expectation and consolidates quantification into relational reasoning.
sourceClaims: Year 2 pupils choose and use appropriate standard units to estimate and measure mass (kg/g) to the nearest appropriate unit using scales, and compare/order mass recording with >, <, =.
learnerActions: Weigh or read several objects and record each mass with its unit.
Decide which is heavier and which is lighter, and put the objects in order by mass.
Record comparisons using the symbols >, < and = (e.g. 300 g > 200 g).
Explain a comparison aloud, e.g. 'the red bag is heavier because 300 g is more than 200 g'.
activities.intendedInsight: Once masses are quantified in the same unit, objects can be compared and ordered numerically and recorded with comparison symbols.

constraints: Units must be identical when counting; mixing unit sizes breaks the count and must be caught before reading.
Wait for the balance beam to settle before reading — a tipping beam is not yet balanced.
Reading a scale means valuing the interval first, then counting intervals (spaces) to the pointer; read to the nearest graduation when the pointer is between marks.
Comparisons and ordering are only valid when the same unit is used throughout.

A short selected-response check (read-the-dial, fill in 'the book = ___ cubes', spot the 'more cubes must be heavier' error, order objects by reading) can check whether the ideas have landed, but it does not by itself provide the hands-on balancing and unit-swap experience; use it alongside, not instead of, actual measuring.

A static labelled dial with a reveal of 'each mark = 100 g' can support interval-reading practice, but it cannot show the live balancing or the count changing when the unit is swapped; reserve the dynamic unit-swap for a setting where the same object can be re-measured.
Estimate before measuring so the measured count can be compared against a prediction.
Standard-unit (g/kg) and symbol-comparison work reflects Year 2 expectations above the stated 5–6 age band; treat it as an extension built on the non-standard balancing foundation.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original source row asserted that a 3D balance 'adds nothing' over a 2D one and that 'dialogue cannot supply' the practice. These are catalog-preference claims not established by the cited sources; they have been removed. A physical (tactile) balance and a screen model offer different experiences, and discussion can support reasoning about why the count changes — only the measure-and-read practice specifically needs an actual balance and scale.

The inverse relationship (larger unit → fewer units) and the marks-vs-intervals reading principle are supported by the cited progression and curriculum documents at the level of general principle, not as evidence that these specific tasks were tested.

Note on terminology: the topic title pairs 'mass' and 'weight'. For these age 5–6 activities the quantity measured and balanced is mass; 'weight' is used colloquially as children often say it. No change was made to the pedagogy/assessment fields.

The Year 2 standard-units/comparison claim was removed from the non-standard cube-balancing activity and from the dial-reading activity because it supports standard-unit choice, estimation and symbol comparison (activity 4), not those activities' specific equivalence and interval-valuing principles; the NCETM dial/scale-reading claim is retained on the reading activity as support for the convention of reading graduated scales.

probeDeeper: 'You said the book is 5 big cubes but 12 small cubes — can both be right? How?'
'If you measured with really TINY cubes, would the number be bigger or smaller? Why?' (inverse relationship, fresh case)
'On the dial, how did you know this mark means 100 g and not 1 g?'
assess.correctAnswer: (1) Balances the book against identical, consistently-placed cubes and reports 'N cubes' with the unit. (2) Explains bigger cubes are heavier, so FEWER of them balance the same book — the count changed because the unit changed, not the book. (3) Values each interval (100 g) and counts intervals to the pointer, e.g. 300 g, rather than counting marks.

errorPatterns.pattern: Unit-size ignorance — counts units without regard to their size ('15 small cubes is heavier than 10 big cubes because 15 > 10')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Balance one big cube against several small cubes so the child sees one big = many small; insist on identical units; connect to 'larger unit → fewer units'.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On task 2 claims the bigger-cube count means a heavier/different book, or compares objects using different-sized cubes

errorPatterns.pattern: Reads a scale by counting marks rather than valuing intervals; can't read a pointer that falls between graduations
errorPatterns.nextMove: Establish what ONE interval is worth first, then count intervals (spaces) not marks to the pointer — exactly as with a ruler; read to the nearest graduation.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On task 3 counts the lines to get the number, or is stuck when the pointer is between marks

errorPatterns.pattern: Doesn't balance cleanly — reads before the beam settles, or unwittingly mixes unit sizes
errorPatterns.nextMove: Wait for the beam to level; check every unit is the same before counting — a procedural prompt, not a concept reteach.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Reports a count while the balance is still tipping, or grabs a mix of cube sizes without noticing

responseLevels.gap: Counts units ignoring their size and/or reads a scale by counting marks; treats more units as always heavier.
responseLevels.full: Quantifies mass with identical units, explains that a larger unit gives a smaller count for the same object, and reads a graduated scale by valuing the intervals and counting them to the pointer.
responseLevels.partial: Measures with identical units and reads simple labelled scales, but is thrown when the unit changes (can't explain the different count) or when the pointer falls between graduations.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child a balance, identical cubes, a set of larger cubes, a book, and a dial scale marked every 100 g. Watch how they work: (1) 'Use the balance and these cubes to find how many cubes this book weighs.' (2) 'Sam measured the same book with these bigger cubes and got a different number — why?' (3) 'Read the dial — what is the mass of this bag?'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Item 2 catches unit-size ignorance — the child who thinks more cubes always means heavier can't explain the different count; item 3 catches the marks-vs-intervals scale-reading error, structurally the same slip as reading a ruler.
